title: Sable: A Small-Field Sumcheck Argument for Bit-Exact Inference of Large Language Models
authors: Tomer Solberg
abstract: We present Sable, an argument system and single-GPU prover for the statement that a committed, integer-quantized transformer produced a given token sequence from a given prompt, bit for bit. title: REAL Loss: Optimizing Real Expected Acceptance Length for Speculative Decoding
authors: Yu Tian
abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates LLM inference by having a draft model propose multiple tokens for the target model to verify in one pass. The speedup is governed by the expected acceptance length (EAL), yet standard training objectives such as cross-entropy, KL divergence, and total variation focus only on distribution matching or single-step overlap. Recent studies instead propose block-level training objectives, aiming to optimize EAL directly. However, these objectives remain surrogates rather than exact formulations of EAL. For example, some average later acceptance over target-distributed continuations rather than the verification branches selected by accepted tokens, introducing a covariance gap that can reverse the gradient direction. title: Tri-Stack-PIM: A Heterogeneous Multi-Die 3D-Integrated Processing-in-Memory Architecture for Efficient LLM Inference
authors: Shuao Jia; Zichao Ling; Chen Bai; Kang Zhao; Jianwang Zhai
abstract: Large language model (LLM) inference during autoregressive decoding is fundamentally memory-bandwidth-bound. title: Deterministic, Reproducible Inference in Exact Integer Arithmetic, and Verifiable Distributed Inference as Its Consequence
authors: Sayed Amir Karim
abstract: Optimized floating-point inference is not reproducible across environments: the same model on different hardware, compilers or thread counts can produce different bits. authors: Jaeyong Song; Daniel Wang; Pratyush Patel; Jonny Kong; Preyas Shah; Shobhit Kanaujia
abstract: Parallel drafters accelerate LLM decoding by proposing a whole block of draft tokens in a single forward pass, making them attractive for LLM serving. title: Inference Validation for Regulated AI: Building a Decision Pipeline on NVIDIA AIPerf
authors: Dev Akre; Roman Bobalo; Manoj Dobbali
abstract: Deploying large language models in regulated industries requires more than picking the fastest inference engine: it requires evidence that a configuration meets contractual and legal obligations before it serves a single customer request. We describe Runway, an internal validation harness built at MasterControl that builds a governed decision pipeline around NVIDIA AIPerf. The key insight is separating concerns: AIPerf provides the trusted measurement, while Runway provides the experiment design that comes before it and the compliance, cost, and audit decisions that come after. We describe the architecture and the storage model that makes caching and audit one mechanism. We report three findings from Runway sweeps: TensorRT-LLM and vLLM rankings invert with concurrency; a newer, pricier GPU instance can be the cheaper one per request; and speculative decoding behaves differently across engines under load, so engine configuration can outweigh engine choice.

abstract: In this work, we study whether frontier agent can continually improve real-world AI infrastructure over long horizons. We evaluate six models across 150 runs with 24-hour budgets, totaling over 10,000 GPU-hours. Our results show that model rankings vary with the evaluation horizon, while 135 of the 150 runs achieve further improvements during the second half of their budgets. These findings indicate that shorter evaluations can overlook both optimization gains and changes in relative model performance. Analysis of agent trajectories identifies task violations, unreliable testing, and premature completion as barriers to sustained improvement. Together, Our Infrathon framework provide resources for constructing long-horizon tasks, evaluating frontier agents, and discovering good infrastructure solutions.

title: $Σ$-LeWM: Learning World Models via S-Information for Robot Control
authors: Xinrui Zu; Michael Przystupa; Zhao Yang; Shujian Yu; Kevin Sebastian Luck
abstract: World models have increasingly been applied as a model-based control method for robotics tasks such as manipulation and locomotion. authors: Nikita Sarawgi; Omey M. Manyar; Satyandra K. Gupta
abstract: Efficient robotic 3D reconstruction requires selecting views that contribute new surface measurements with few physical captures. The adapted method recovers a surface region that the nominal method repeatedly targets but fails to measure. These results suggest that robots can reuse pretrained predictive models while adapting their decisions to local operating conditions in data-scarce environments.

title: Library of Hands: Fix the Hands, Not the World Model
authors: Hasaan Ahmad; Qizhen Ying; Yuxuan Sun; Tianjin Huang; Guangming Wang
abstract: A world model predicts how a scene changes after an action, and a planner uses it to search for actions that reach a goal. If the camera moves or the controller changes, the same command moves the robot differently: when its commands are turned by 90 degrees, a frozen planner with the LeWM world model that succeeds in 77.5% of episodes succeeds in only 7.8%. Current fixes retrain the model, need training data, or forget a set-up when it returns. We propose Library of Hands (LoH), a training-free method that keeps the world model frozen and corrects only the map from commands to applied actions, which we call the hand. LoH reads the hand through the frozen model, with no extra sensor: it finds the action that best explains the change between two camera images (a reading). It stores every hand it identifies, so a returning set-up is recognised rather than re-learnt. In closed-loop tests, LoH more than doubles success on three simulated tasks, from 28.6% to 62.3%, and loses only 0.6 percentage points when nothing changes. It also works, unchanged, with two other world models and on two of three models pretrained on real robot data, and its gain grows with the quality of its readings.

title: Coverage-Verified Sparse Attention: Closed-Loop Quality Control for Long-Context LLM Decoding
authors: Yan-Cheng Li; Chun-Yi Lee
abstract: Sparse attention accelerates long-context decoding by reading a subset of the KV cache, but existing methods are open-loop: the kernel commits to its selection with no signal indicating whether enough attention mass was preserved and no recovery path when it was not. title: LongCapHarness: Capability-Guided Auto-Harnessing for Long-Context Reasoning
authors: Tao Zhang; Yuhang He
abstract: Existing methods enhancing an LLM's long-context reasoning capability often rely on data synthesis and follow-up LLM post-training. The harnessing process recursively revises and updates capability primitive implementation, capability state and control logic through recursive self-improvement on the development set. title: PACE: Keeping the Right Tokens in the KV Cache Is Not Enough for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
authors: Suman Chatterjee
abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents accumulate sessions of up to millions of tokens, far more key-value (KV) cache than one GPU holds, so serving systems keep a small budget of tokens and evict the rest. authors: Dayou Du; Woon Yee Ng; Guangming Sheng; Nick Lau; Jianyi Cheng; Luo Mai
abstract: The key-value (KV) cache dominates memory capacity and bandwidth in long-context LLM serving. authors: Huzaifa Pardawala; Siddhant Sukhani; Sudheer Chava; Agam Shah
abstract: Context selection can reduce input length during long-input inference but can remove evidence required to answer a query. title: CoRD: Coupled Rollouts Fill the Blind Spot of On-Policy Distillation
authors: Guhan Chen; Bohan Li; Jun Rao; Hejin Wang; Songtao Tian; Yexin Xie; Xiaojun Meng; Peng Yuan; Jiansheng Wei; Xuebo Liu; Zixiong Yu
abstract: On-policy distillation trains a student on its own rollouts, so states the teacher would reach but the student does not are seldom supervised. We introduce CoRD (coupled-rollout distillation), which keeps the on-policy loss and moves only the distribution of training states toward the teacher, drawing rollouts from a geometric interpolation of student and teacher through the maximal coupling of speculative decoding. The coupling keeps the student's token wherever the two distributions agree and otherwise substitutes a token from the part of the target the student underweights, so interventions are as rare as any exact sampler allows and recede as the student learns. Across six base students from two model families (Qwen3 and Qwen3.5, 0.6B to 4B), CoRD raises average pass@1 over on-policy distillation by 0.9 to 2.0 points and pass@8 by 1.2 to 3.4 points on five public math benchmarks at equal steps and data. On frozen teacher-reached states, a 4B student trained with CoRD reaches in 16 steps a gap closure that on-policy distillation does not reach in 80, and substitution rules intervening at least as often in other directions fall short of CoRD.
